links.reason: The verse is her own letter, where she says she painted and garlanded Civakan's image (உருவுதீட்டித் தொங்கல்வேய்ந்து தொழுதாற்ற); it is a plea (மகளிர்காம மறைத்தொழிதியோ), not a story that tests the quatrain. No hostile frame appears in the verse, and her constancy is only self-reported.

The friend's argument is sores, eyes and caste (புண்களுங் கண்கள் கொள்ளாச் சாதியும்), not the bag-turned-inside-out meditation of the quatrain. That the remedy fails comes from later verses, not this one.

759 calls the kings ஆரிரை (food) for his arrows, and 798 has him invite them as guests and feed (ஊட்டினான்) each one or two arrows. The later verse carries out the earlier figure, and the note describes both ends accurately.

The note says only the dharma's austerity loosens the deed, but 321 says no such thing; it says the killing does not end (தீர்ந்திடாக் கொலை) and follows through births. TM 200 is a list of sins given up on reaching Siva's feet, so the two do not claim opposite things about the same point.

The figurative letter (ஓடரி நெடுங்கண்ணென்னும் ஓலை) in 683 and the written one (ஓலை மரபினீட்ட) in 2586 are a real pair, but 2586 shows only that the letter is handed over. That it makes the same appeal in words, or that love must now be answered openly, is not in the verse.

Both name Kapilar and மாவண் பாரி. 236 asks fate to let him live with Pari in the next birth, and 61 has Pari gone to the far land (வாராச் சேண்புலம் படர்ந்தோன்) and the poet drawn to a new patron by a fame for giving without regret (ஈத்தது இரங்கான்). The pair does show two answers to the patron's death, though the Chera's praise being an elegy is a mild stretch.

Verse 174 does have the mother reborn as a dog (தாய்...நாய்) killing the peacock, and the narrator names the fruit of harmful deeds. The mother meeting her child is not in the verse, where neither recognises the other, and the peacock-as-son and the doer's identity depend on plot outside it.

152 says nothing about who made the bond; it lists a path through fast, worship of the arhats and gifts to Indra's rank, kingship and release. TM 432 says the Lord shut the soul in the bond. They answer different questions, so the tension is manufactured.

Both describe hell torture, but neither extends the other. 2774 names no sin (its cause comes in later verses), and 198 puts those who said 'kill, stab' in fire-mouthed hell. Importing 198's sin into 2774 mixes a Jain sermon with a Saiva verse, so only the shared theme remains.

The goad is shared (வயிரத் தோட்டி against உரனென்னும் தோட்டி), and the goad of awareness on the elephant of knowledge is a real match. The note's army and karmic enemy and 'assault' are not in 2113, which says only that it drives along the sacred texts and the mind.
This is plot order: the summons, then the women's reaction (மன்னவன் குறிப்பு நோக்கி). 2923 does not say the intent is a farewell, so 'his intent is a farewell' is supplied from outside the verse.

The contrast between the unmoved victor (உவந்திலன் வியந்திலன்) and the laughing soldier (நகும்) is real. But the Kural's laugh comes mid-fight at a wound, while 726 is a calm report after killing a lion, so the mood contrast is thin and neither side gains something specific.

Vijayai names her own deeds (நல்வினை செய்திலாதேன்) and still sobs (விம்மா), which shows that naming one's deeds does not by itself give the calm Naladiyar 33 promises the wise. The verse sits between the quatrain's fool and wise, so qualifies fits, though her grief is partly for her son.

The link rests on the number seven (எழுவர் காறு against எழுமை எழுபிறப்பு). The contrast of grounds, fate and inherited kinship against gratitude for rescue, is true, but the 'measure of what the bond is owed' gain names nothing specific.

Kantukkatan's reasoning (வேந்தொடு மாறு கோடல் விளிகுற்றார் தொழில்) matches the couplet's prudence, but it is a character's reasoning, not a test of the rule. The epic does not show a cost of submission or weigh it, so the verse illustrates the couplet.

The crows and kites kept off with a stick (காக்கை கைத்தடி) do appear in both, and the shared body-as-carrion picture is real. Beyond that the teaches only says the picture was fixed, and the gains are trivial.

Honour bringing fruit with neither favour nor anger (அருளும் முனிவும் இலர்) set against grace in the measure of praise is a defensible contrast. But line 4 (கடவுளர் செயலே) puts the course of the world in the divine ones' doing, so the claim that the verse has no giver is not secure.

The waiting in 359 and the arrival in 1909 (நம்பி வந்தனன்) are a real pair. But 359 has her watching for the companion's return, not for news of her son, and 'a watch that began at his birth' is not in either verse.

Sil 7 praises Kaveri for not sulking (புலவாது ஒழிதல்) as a wife's virtue, while 650 only describes a cuckoo coaxing back a mate who turned away. 650 does not say the sulk is just or that the woman should sulk, so these are different situations, not a conflict.

Both mothers recall the nochchi (நொச்சி) after the girl's elopement, one forgotten by the girl and one unbearable to the mother. That contrast is real, but neither poem extends the other, so this is a shared image.
This is story sequence: the hunters surround him (117) and fire the wood (119). The teaches speaks of arrows, which neither verse mentions, and nothing is answered or reversed.

The verse turns the Buddhist definition of evil as pain-causing (தீவினை...உழப்பு) on the Buddha. That is a reductio, which applies the causer-bears-pain principle rather than limiting it. The claim that only a theory of what makes a deed evil can stop it is not in the verse.

Kannaki blames strong karma (வல்வினை வந்துருத்த) and calls herself கடுவினையேன், which agrees with the couplet's ஊழ் priority. Her burning of Madurai is not in these lines, so the claim that she keeps it as her own deed is unsupported.

The link rests on the shared words feet and flower. 1037 likens worshippers to lotuses opening at the Jina's feet, while Kural 3 promises long life to those who reach the Lord's feet, and the verse is a simile with no promise to qualify.
The scene matches the couplet closely: a gaze, then the accusation of thinking of others (பிறரை உள்ளி அழுபவர்). But the verse ends with her anguish (வேதனை பெருகி), so 'ends in laughter' is not in it.

Line 3 grants victory to fate (வெல்வது விதியினாகும்) and then stakes his honour on not blinking at a spear (வேல்வரின் இமைப்பேனாயின்), which is Kural 775's test of valour. Separating outcome from courage is true of the verse; the 'one part fate cannot take' is mild extrapolation.

The verse says only that five ascetics end as gods (தேவராயினார்). That heaven is not the last goal comes from the Kural alone, and nothing in the verse says they had not cut off pride, so the epic adds nothing to the couplet.

Both urge acting before death, but 2616 has no hiccup; its image is the cow being milked (கறந்துகூற்றுண்ணு ஞான்று). The cost-of-hearing-it-at-the-wrong-moment claim is not in the verse, which makes this agreement.

The prince's oath sends away the elephants and warriors (யானை...தொழிலாளரும் தவிர்க), which sets aside the allies' strength Kural 471 counts. But 'to keep his word' and the going alone rest on 709, and the verse's sense is flagged uncertain.

Both show a battlefield with ghouls and jackals, but Pur 369 does not lead to 804 or build on it. That the ghouls take the bard's role and sing thanks is the proposer's reading of அளித்தவை பாடி, and the gains are speculative.
149 has the soul leave the body by dharma meditation (தியானந்தன்னால் மேனி விட்டு) and become a god, but it uses no sleep or waking image. Making the couplet's simile literal is the proposer's gloss.
Vikraman gives up his kingdom and becomes a forest ascetic, but 23 gives no reason or sign of seeing impermanence. The epic's 'reason' comes from the quatrain, so the verse only illustrates it.

201 lists discerning true things (மெய்ப்பொருள் தெரிதல்), knowledge and conduct as the Lord's teaching, which does place seeing first in a larger course. The couplet does not claim seeing is the whole of release, so little is qualified, and the link rests partly on the shared word மெய்ப்பொருள்.
The pair is a shared theme of acting before grey hair (கருந்தலைகள் வெண்டலைகளாய்... நரைவரும்). The staff and the widowed speaker in the gains are not in the epic verse.

The reversal depends on reading வறமழை as literal rain sent by the sages, but the marked reading is a rain of virtue, so the reversal rests on a doubtful word. The gains about relieving the distress that stops giving are speculative.

The narrator says the false name was not a lie (பொய்ந்நாட்டேனும் பொய்யல ஆற்றால்), which is the exception of Kural 292, and the pair shows whether 'faultless good' fits a lie for safety. The note's fugitive-from-usurper context comes from outside the verse, which is a small flaw.

The dream of the asoka falling with a shoot rising from its foot (பிண்டி தொலைந்து...முளை ஓங்குபு) is fulfilled in 313, where the queen has lost the kingdom (அரசு அழிய) and gained a son (புதல்வன் பெற்று), and the poet gives sun-set and crescent-moon as the figure. The reference to 225 is outside the packet but not needed.
The shared words are generic karma terms (நல்வினை). 1054 is a friends' remark on the wedding day and 1057 a night simile, so nothing distinctive is shared.
These are two verses of one hell catalogue, blades in 2764 and a boiling froth in 2770, in sermon order. Neither answers or reverses the other, so the connection is sequence.

308 shows the king weary of pleasure and going to bow to Vamana (வெறுத்து...அடிதொழும்), not leaving. The couplet's condition, household life in virtue, is not tested, so there is no case here of a successful householder who leaves.

899 is a vow that he come defeated and worship her anklet feet (சிலம்படி கைதொழ), and 2012 is the disguised Civakan begging milk-rice at her gate. That is an ironic reversal, but he does not worship her feet, so 'fulfilled to the letter' is overstated.

The king gives up kingship at ease (இனிதியல்பினமர்ந்திருக்கும் அளவில்) and rises to austerity, which fits renouncing while it exists. The couplet is not about haste and the verse gives no cost of haste, so the teaches is not in either text.

Line 2 says there is no restraint if desire rises (நிறையென்பதில்லை காமம்...பெருகுமாயின்), which is Kural 1251. Lines 3-4 qualify it by saying her rare restraint was not broken but went to the fragrant-haired lord (நம்பிபாற் பட்டதன்றே), the one thing the couplet does not say.
